title: Kazakhstan Again Sentences Activists for Supposed Attempt to Seize Power
gist: On September 8, an Almaty court sentenced five men, several with activist backgrounds, to five to five-and-a-half years for allegedly attempting to seize power, organizing mass unrest and seizing the Akorda presidential residence; activists say such closed-door cases are a government strategy to control opposition.

insights.claim: On September 8, 2026, an Almaty court sentenced five men to between five and five-and-a-half years in prison for allegedly advocating violent seizure of power, organizing mass unrest, and planning to seize the Akorda presidential residence.
insights.speaker: Albert Otkjær
insights.so_what: Continued use of coup-plot charges signals a tightening political climate in Kazakhstan relevant to governance risk assessments.

insights.claim: Several of those convicted had histories of activism and participation in civil protests, and the hearings were held behind closed doors.
insights.speaker: Albert Otkjær
insights.so_what: Closed trials of activists weaken rule-of-law perceptions for foreign investors in Kazakhstan.
insights.locator: Several of the convicted have a past

insights.claim: Activists and national human rights organizations argue that such court cases are part of a Kazakh government strategy to control the opposition, pointing to similar earlier cases.
insights.speaker: Albert Otkjær
insights.so_what: Recurring politically-driven prosecutions suggest stability is maintained through repression rather than reform, a latent risk if protests recur.
insights.quote: These types of court cases, activists argue, are part of a strategy employed by the Kazakh government to control opposition in the country.
insights.locator: Several of the convicted have a past
